title: One in three teen boys follows Andrew Tate at least a little, and those who do hold more rigid views of manhood ho-do-hold-more-rigid-views-of-manhood/
author: Eric W. Dolan
summary: Eric Dolan reports on a survey of 601 American boys aged 13 to 17, led by Erica Scharrer with L. Monique Ward and Brenda Volling and published in Psychology of Men & Masculinities. About a third said they follow Andrew Tate at least a little and 11.6 percent follow Jordan Peterson, yet only about 9 percent named a manosphere figure as a favourite personality. Boys who followed these figures held more traditional beliefs about toughness, dominance, and emotional detachment, and this held for Tate even after controlling for age, self-perceived masculinity, and parental messages. Parental messages about being big and tough were the strongest predictor, carrying two to three times the weight of following Tate. Following manosphere figures was not associated with greater depression, hostility, or lower support, which cuts against the picture of isolated boys drifting toward these influencers. The article stresses that the survey is a single snapshot and cannot show causation. Included here as an expansion of Anthony Bradley's weekly digest.
points: About a third of surveyed teen boys follow Tate at least a little, but very few name a manosphere figure as a favourite, so exposure is wider than devotion.
Following Tate predicted more traditional masculinity beliefs on every scale even after controlling for parental messages and self-perceived masculinity.
Parents' messages about being big and tough were the strongest predictor in every model, which points to the home as a primary teacher of masculine norms.
Boys who followed these figures were not more depressed, hostile, or less supported, contrary to the isolated-boy narrative.
The cross-sectional design cannot separate influence from selection, so the findings show association rather than cause.
quotes: Teenage boys who follow prominent online personalities associated with the “manosphere” are more likely to support traditional beliefs about manhood, such as the idea that men should hide their emotions, remain dominant, and reject anything considered feminine.

In contrast, when asked open-ended questions about their absolute favorite personalities, only about 9 percent wrote in a figure associated with the manosphere, most commonly naming mainstream creators, musicians, or athletes instead. The authors described it as encouraging that only a small share of participants named a manosphere figure among their favorites.
The authors note that this runs counter to the idea that isolated or distressed boys are the ones who turn to the manosphere.

Parental messages about being big and tough were the strongest predictor in every model, carrying roughly two to three times the weight of following Tate, and following Peterson was a weaker predictor than following Tate.

Following Jordan Peterson also predicted higher support for male toughness, dominance, and relationship-specific masculinity norms, though it did not predict anti-femininity beliefs. The authors suggest this may reflect Peterson’s emphasis on self-improvement rather than overtly anti-women messaging.

Our study cannot show causality, but our data do show that in our sample of teen boys, following manosphere influencers online goes hand in hand with having narrow, stereotypical conceptions of masculinity,” Scharrer noted.

The study relies on survey responses gathered at a single point in time, meaning the scientists cannot determine whether watching these creators causes boys to adopt traditional beliefs, or if boys who already favor traditional roles simply seek out compatible media.
